title: pH curves; Buffers
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB07#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB07#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB07#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB07#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB07#N.4b, AB09#N.4b, AB07#N.9, AB09#N.6b, AB07#N.12, AB09#N.11b, AB07#N.13, AB09#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Half-equivalence
items.clue: The stage of a titration at which [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

items.label: Buffer region
items.clue: Gentle slope before the steep section, where HA and A⁻ are both present.

items.label: Equivalence point
items.clue: The middle of the steep section of a pH curve, where amounts match the equation.

items.label: Methyl orange
items.clue: Indicator changing at about pH 3–4.5, chosen for a strong acid with a weak base.

questions.stem: A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HA, a weak monoprotic acid, with 0.10 M NaOH and finds that the pH at the half-equivalence point is 4.70. The student then titrates 25.0 mL of 0.010 M HA with 0.010 M NaOH at the same temperature. How does the pH at the half-equivalence point of the second titration compare with that of the first?

options.text: It is higher by about one pH unit
It is higher by about half a pH unit
It is unchanged from the first titration
It is lower than in the first titration

questions.explanation: [HA] = [A⁻] at half-equivalence, so pH = pKa. Dilution changes both concentrations equally, and pKa is constant at a given temperature: still 4.70.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of the two solutions in each pair are mixed at 25°C. Which mixture is a buffer solution?
questions.explanation: The NaOH converts half the CH₃COOH to CH₃COO⁻, leaving large, equal concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the equilibrium that determines the pH at the equivalence point of the titration of CH₃COOH(aq) with NaOH(aq)?
questions.explanation: At the equivalence point the CH₃COOH has been converted to CH₃COO⁻. This conjugate base accepts protons from water, producing OH⁻, so this equilibrium sets the (basic) pH.

questions.stem: A buffer at 25°C contains 0.15 M NH₃ and 0.30 M NH₄Cl. The pKa of NH₄⁺ is 9.25. What is the pH of the buffer?
questions.explanation: NH₄⁺ is the acid, NH₃ the base: pH = 9.25 + log(0.15/0.30) = 9.25 − 0.30 = 8.95.

questions.stem: A solution of a weak diprotic acid, H₂A, is titrated with NaOH(aq). The pH at the first equivalence point is 8.5. Which species, other than H₂O and Na⁺, is present at the highest concentration at the first equivalence point?
questions.explanation: The OH⁻ added has removed one proton from every H₂A, so HA⁻ is the major species. Only small amounts of H₂A and A²⁻ form from it.

questions.stem: A buffer is made from CH₃COOH and NaCH₃COO. Which quantity sets the maximum amount of HCl that the buffer can neutralize before its pH begins to fall sharply?

options.text: The pH of the buffer itself
The Ka of the acetic acid

questions.explanation: Added H₃O⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻ 1 : 1, so the moles of CH₃COO⁻ set how much HCl the buffer can neutralize.

questions.stem: Separate 20.0 mL portions of 0.100 M NaOH(aq) and of 0.100 M base B(aq) are each titrated with 0.100 M HCl(aq). Both need 20.0 mL of acid. Which feature of the curves shows that B is a weak base?

options.text: B's curve needs a larger volume of acid to reach its equivalence point than the NaOH curve does.
B's curve starts at a lower pH, falls gently at first, and reaches equivalence below pH 7.
B's curve has no steep section at all, because a weak base reacts with the acid only partly.
B's curve reaches its equivalence point above pH 7, because B is a base and so stays alkaline.

questions.stem: Inside cells, a buffer of dihydrogenphosphate ions, H₂PO₄⁻, and hydrogenphosphate ions, HPO₄²⁻, helps keep the pH close to 7. A process in the cell releases some OH⁻ ions. Which reaction removes most of the added OH⁻?
questions.explanation: H₂PO₄⁻ is the weak acid of this pair, so it donates H⁺ to the OH⁻. The ratio [H₂PO₄⁻]/[HPO₄²⁻] changes only slightly, so the pH barely moves.
